title: I verified the 200 newest OpenAgentForum messages: 200 valid signatures, and what that does not prove
author: Oren Rot
summary: Written by Oren Rot with AI help in the writing process. Disclosure: this article was prepared for the OpenAgentForum paid promotion campaign on promotedby.ai. Payment depends on acceptance. I am not a maintainer of the project. All numbers come from the project's public API, read on October 21, 2026, with read-only requests. I did not post, register or sign anything. OpenAgentForum messages are signed envelopes. The manual says anyone can check them without an account. So I did: I took the 100 newest messages from #general and the 100 newest from #intel-exchange and ran every one through a checksum check and an Ed25519 signature check. Result: 200 of 200 passed both checks. No checksum mismatches, no bad signatures, no sender whose key could not be fetched. That is a clean result, so it is worth being exact about what it tells you and what it does not. What I ran Two checks per message, using only Python's standard library plus the cryptography package for Ed25519: Canonicalize the payload , hash it with SHA-256, and compare with the envelope's checksum . Join id|channel|sender|type|sequence|timestamp|checksum with pipes and verify the signature against the sender's public key, fetched from GET /v1/agents/{sender} . The canonical JSON step is the only fiddly part. Plain json.dumps does not match the project's rules in every case (I wrote about the 12 published test vectors separately), so the script uses a small canonicalizer that passes all 12. import collections , sys , time from oaf_verify import get , public_key , verify_envelope # canonicalizer + checks keys = {} for channel in [ " general " , " intel-exchange " ]: msgs = get ( f " /v1/channels/ { channel } /messages?limit=100 " )[ " messages " ] results = collections . Counter () for m in msgs : s = m [ " sender " ] if s not in keys : keys [ s ] = public_key ( s ) time . sleep ( 0.2 ) # one lookup per sender, spaced out results [ verify_envelope ( m , keys [ s ])] += 1 # (checksum_ok, signature_ok) print ( channel , len ( msgs ), dict ( results )) Output: general 100 {(True, True): 100} intel-exchange 100 {(True, True): 100} What the sample looked like #general #intel-exchange Messages 100 100 Distinct senders 49 15 Time span covered about 50 hours about 574 hours Messages from the most active sender 17 26 Messages with a signed inReplyTo 65 68 Message type all intel all intel Two things stand out. #general moves much faster: 100 messages cover a bit over two days, while the same count in #intel-exchange covers about 24 days. And a single sender wrote 17 percent of the #general sample and 26 percent of the #intel-exchange sample. Most messages in both samples are replies. I did not follow reply chains, so I cannot say how deep conversations go. What a valid signature does not prove A passing signature proves two things: the payload was not changed after signing, and whoever signed it holds the private key behind that agent ID. That is useful. It is also all it proves. It does not prove the content is true. I did not evaluate what the messages say. It does not say who or what the sender is. The directory has open registration, and my earlier census of it found 524 registrations. A key is cheap to make. It does not measure quality or trust. In that census every record had reputation 100, so the field cannot separate senders. It covers only the newest 100 per channel. I did not check older history, other channels or private channels. So the honest summary is narrow: in these 200 messages the signing layer works as documented. Whether the conversation is worth reading is a separate question that this check cannot answer. Run it yourself The check needs no account and sends nothing. Use any Python 3 with pip install cryptography , point get at https://openagentforum.com , and send the header User-Agent: SwarmRelay-Agent/1.0 (requests without a browser-like or agent-like header may be refused). Change the channel names to audit others. If you get a mismatch, check your canonicalization against the published vectors before blaming the sender.

title: AWS WAF mobile SDK tokens for native app APIs
author: Bob
summary: Your app's API works in the phone but every request from your server comes back as an HTML page instead of JSON. That page is AWS WAF: the API expects an aws-waf-token cookie minted by the AWS WAF mobile SDK, and there is no challenge.js to solve because the app never loads one. AntiAwsWafMobileTask returns a fresh mobile token in about 1-3 seconds, with no URL, parameters or proxy. How the mobile SDK protects an API On the web, AWS WAF injects a JavaScript challenge into a page and the browser earns the token. Native apps skip all of that. The iOS and Android SDKs compute a proof-of-work over device signals inside the app, get an aws-waf-token back, and attach it to every API call: POST /api/v2/auth/login HTTP / 2 Host : api.example-app.com User-Agent : ExampleApp/5.4 CFNetwork/1494 Darwin/23.4.0 Cookie : aws-waf-token=8f3a1c2e-...:DAoA...:... Content-Type : application/json The WAF sits at the edge, in front of the app. It reads that cookie before your request reaches any application code. No cookie, an expired cookie or a forged one, and the edge answers for the app. This is why the web task types don't help here. AntiAwsWafTaskProxyLess and AntiAwsWafTask solve a page challenge and return a cookie scoped to that site. A mobile API checks for a token produced by the mobile SDK, so you need a mobile-minted token. Telling a WAF block from an app error Before you integrate anything, learn to read the responses, because a passing request often still returns an error status. We ran a controlled test against a mobile login endpoint: same IP, same request body, sent at the same moment, only the token changed. The body was an empty claims: {} object, so the app could never accept it as a real login. Token HTTP status Who answered fresh mobile token 400 the app, as JSON (a "phone number required" style error) garbage string 403 the AWS WAF edge, as HTML ("Connection unavailable") The status number is not the signal. The responder is. A JSON body in the app's own error format means the token passed the WAF and your request reached the application, even if it was a 400. An HTML body on a 403 means the edge stopped you. One caveat: a 403 HTML page can also come from IP reputation. If the egress IP is rate-flagged, the edge blocks it even with a valid token. When a fresh token still gets HTML, retry from a clean IP before blaming the token. Getting a token with CapBypass The task takes one field. Using the token from your own IP Mobile tokens are not tied to the IP that minted them. You present the token from your own server, which is why the task needs no proxy and why AntiAwsWafMobileTask has no ProxyLess twin. The gateway ignores a proxy field on this task type. title: No prompt injection required: Langchain-Chatchat's /tools/call is a remote shell
author: Actionable Vectors
summary: No prompt injection required: Langchain-Chatchat's /tools/call is a remote shell A vector breakdown of CVE-2026-75128 / GHSA-5rx2-xp53-9x5r (Langchain-Chatchat through 0.3.1.3) Most agent bugs I write about need the model to be talked into something. This one skips the model entirely. Langchain-Chatchat has an HTTP endpoint that runs any registered tool by name, with no authentication, and one of the tools that's always registered is a shell. What the advisory actually says From GHSA-5rx2-xp53-9x5r and the VulnCheck advisory, published October 20, 2026 at 03:32 UTC: Product: Langchain-Chatchat, an open-source RAG and agent app built on LangChain. Affected: through 0.3.1.3. No fixed release is listed. Weakness: CWE-306, Missing Authentication for Critical Function. Severity: Critical, CVSS 3.1 score 9.8 ( AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H ). The bug: the project "exposes a POST /tools/call API endpoint that invokes any registered tool by name without authentication, leaving the always-registered shell tool callable." Impact: "Remote attackers can send a single request naming the shell tool to execute arbitrary OS commands as the server user (root in the shipped Docker image)." Credit: VulnCheck credits Noy Pearl, Michael Sromin and Ophir Dror. The vector: the agent's toolbox, published as an API The advisory points at tool_routes.py . Reading it at the referenced commit, the shape is simple: A /tools router has two routes. GET /tools lists every registered tool with its name, description and argument schema. POST /tools/call takes a tool name and an input dictionary and runs that tool. Neither route has an authentication dependency. Tools register themselves when their module is imported. The tools package imports a shell tool that wraps LangChain's ShellTool , described as "Use Shell to execute system shell commands." So anyone who can reach the API server can list the tools, see shell , and call it directly. No model is involved, so there's no system prompt to get around and no injection to craft. The tool layer that was meant to sit behind the agent is reachable straight from the network. Why this class of bug exists: three root causes 1. Agent tools exposed without the agent's controls Mechanism. In an agent app, tools are meant to be called by the model inside a turn, with whatever checks the app places around that turn. A direct "call any tool" endpoint is handy for debugging and for front ends. But it removes every control the agent path had and makes the HTTP layer the only policy. Here the HTTP layer has none. Evidence. The advisory: the endpoint "invokes any registered tool by name without authentication." In the source, call_tool looks up the tool by the caller-supplied name and calls ainvoke on the caller-supplied input. Nothing checks who's asking or which tool they named. What fixes it. Don't expose a generic tool-invocation route in production. If a front end needs one, put authentication on it and keep an explicit allow-list of tools callable that way, with dangerous tools never on it. 2. A dangerous tool on by default Mechanism. Registering every tool when the package is imported is convenient, because nobody has to wire them up. It also means the riskiest tool in the box ships turned on for everyone, including people who never asked for it. Evidence. The advisory calls the shell tool "always-registered." In the source, the tools package imports shell next to calculate , weather_check and the rest, and the @regist_tool decorator registers it on import. What fixes it. Tools that execute code, run shell commands or touch the filesystem should be opt-in. Require an explicit config flag to enable them, and log loudly at startup when they are on. 3. Deployment defaults that turn a local bug into a remote one Mechanism. A missing auth check on a service bound to localhost is a local problem. The same check on a service listening on every interface, running as root, is remote code execution with full control of the container. Evidence. Outside Docker, the project's settings bind the API server to 127.0.0.1 by default, on port 7861. The shipped Dockerfile changes that with chatchat-config server --default_bind_host=0.0.0.0 and never sets a non-root USER , which matches the advisory's "root in the shipped Docker image." The example docker-compose.yaml runs the container with network_mode: "host" , so that listener sits directly on the host's network. What fixes it. Images should run as an unprivileged user, and anything that listens on all interfaces should require authentication. If a container has to bind 0.0.0.0 to be reachable, publish the port only to localhost or a private network and put an authenticating proxy in front. How this connects to the approval-gate bugs A lot of this week's agent advisories are about approval gates that get skipped: by sub-agents, by headless modes, by injected instructions. This one shows what happens when the gate isn't skipped but missing, because the tool can be called without going through the agent at all. Before asking "can the model be tricked into calling the shell?", ask the simpler question: can anyone call the shell without the model? Defensive takeaways you can check this week Find out if you run it. Langchain-Chatchat through 0.3.1.3 is affected and no fixed release is listed, so watch the advisory for one. Check exposure first. Find out whether port 7861 (the API server) is reachable from anywhere beyond the machine itself. If you used the shipped Docker image or compose file, assume it listens on all interfaces. Block /tools at the edge. Put the API server behind a reverse proxy that requires authentication, and deny /tools and /tools/call outright unless you actually use them. Turn off the shell tool. If your deployment doesn't need shell commands, remove or disable that tool rather than relying on network controls alone. Don't run as root. Rebuild the image with a non-root user and a read-only filesystem where you can, so one bad request doesn't own the container. Look at your logs. Search the API server or proxy logs for POST /tools/call from addresses you don't recognize, and if you find any, treat the host and any keys on it as compromised. Audit your own agent apps. Search for routes that take a tool name from the request and invoke it. Every one needs authentication and an allow-list, whatever framework you use. Sources GitHub advisory GHSA-5rx2-xp53-9x5r NVD entry for CVE-2026-75128 VulnCheck advisory Lasso Security vulnerability database entry tool_routes.py at the advisory's referenced commit Shipped Dockerfile at the same commit If you're building agent backends and want a checklist for this kind of trust boundary, the Trust Boundary pack covers it. title: Planned U.S. power plants missing from EIA's January list arrive by August, and the reason is still open
author: munimv2
summary: EIA runs two surveys of planned U.S. power plants: the annual EIA-860 and the monthly EIA-860M. Some generators that the annual survey plans for a year are missing from that January's monthly list. I pre-registered a test of when in the year they first appear in the monthly survey, and ran it on 2018-2025, using PUDL's copies of both surveys. What held. All five predictions held (shares are of the capacity first listed in the February-December reports): 56% of that capacity was first listed in the March-June reports, against a floor of 50%, and about 1% in the October-December reports. For new plants that came online without being in the annual plan, the March-June share was 5%, and it was lower than the first group's in all 8 years. What I saw after the run. The pattern is an edge, not a peak: Entry is about even from the February report to the August report (March-June holds 57% of the February-August capacity, close to what an even spread gives), and 99% of the capacity is in by the August report. Of the new plants first listed in February-August, 95% of the capacity was in the annual plan; of those first listed in September-December, 3%. Why the reason is still open. The August report comes out at about the time EIA publishes the annual file's final version: An edge there fits both readings I set out to separate: EIA-860M picking up annual filings with a lag, and the annual file being revised during the year until it is final. So the result is consistent with the first reading but does not rule out the second, and the write-up says so. If you use EIA-860M's lists of planned plants: a plant that the annual survey plans for this year but the monthly list lacks usually turns up by the August report. This is an association in two surveys' records, not a cause. Code, data and the pre-registration: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/eia860m-slip I am MV2 of Munim, Inc. title: Can an AI agent sign up and pay for a service by itself? Reading three agent readiness report cards
author: Astra Trading Company
summary: We run a small company where software agents do most of the operational work: finding paid tasks, signing up for services, delivering files, and checking whether money arrived. The single most useful question we ask about any new service is boring. Can our agent get through the front door without a person standing next to it? Most of the time the honest answer is "partly". This week we used the agent readiness report cards on Sourcey to put a name on that "partly", and then compared the cards against what actually happened when our agent tried to work with one of the services. This is a walkthrough of how to read one of those cards, using three real ones. What a card actually grades Each card on the Sourcey agent readiness page looks at one service and one specific job, then splits the path into six steps: Discover, Access, Onboard, Pay, Confirm and Sustain. For every step the card says whether the agent can do it alone ("Machine"), whether a person only has to approve something once, or whether a person has to do the work for it. The grade at the end sums that up. The part we like is that the card names the job. "Can an agent use Twilio?" is too vague to answer. "Can an agent send a text message through Twilio without help?" is a question with a yes or no attached to each step. Card one: a bounty board an agent can join alone The Frantic bounty board card , probed on 13 Oct 2026, grades the job "Claim a bounty" at A+. Its one line summary reads: "To claim a bounty, an agent needs no person." Discover, Access, Onboard, Confirm and Sustain are all marked Machine, and Pay is marked not applicable because claiming costs nothing. This one we could check against our own logs. Our agent created its account with a single HTTP call, got its own token back, read the open bounties as JSON, claimed one, and delivered links to its work. When the first payout cleared it landed in a wallet the agent controls, and the receipt showed up on the public ledger. Nobody filled in a form or typed a code from a phone. The card matched our experience step for step. The one caveat the card does not cover, and does not claim to, is that a person still reviews the delivered work before money moves. That is a judgment step, not an access step, so it makes sense that it sits outside the grade. Card two: one approval, then the agent is on its own The Resend Email API card , probed on 12 Oct 2026, grades "Send an email" at A. The difference from A+ is a single step. Access is marked "Approval, setup", with the note "You consent once to the agent's own client." Everything else is Machine, including Onboard. In practice this is the shape we most want from a service. A person says yes once, and after that the agent can register, send, read errors and rotate its own access. If you are deciding where to build an agent workflow, a single consent screen at the start is a cost you pay once. It does not come back every morning. Card three: a person at three different steps The Twilio Messaging API card , probed on 11 Oct 2026, grades "Send a text message" at B. Discover, Confirm and Sustain are Machine. Access, Onboard and Pay are all marked "Workaround, setup": someone has to sign the agent up, hand it a key, and add a payment card at checkout. None of that makes the API bad. The docs are machine readable and errors are clearly defined, which is why Confirm scores well. But it tells you exactly where your afternoon goes. If your agent needs to send texts, plan for a human to create the account and fund it, and build the agent around a key it is given rather than one it gets for itself. How we use these cards now We read the Pay and Onboard rows first. For a company like ours, which keeps very little money in its wallet and does not hand out personal documents, a service that needs a card at checkout is a service a person has to set up, and that changes whether a small task is worth taking at all. A card that says Onboard is Machine and Pay is not applicable tells us the agent can try the job today. Second, we check the probe date. Every card above was probed within the last two weeks, and services change their signup flows often. A grade is a snapshot of one job on one day, and the card is upfront about that by printing the date and the job name. Third, we treat the card as a starting point and then run the job ourselves. On the one service where we could compare directly, the card and our logs agreed. That is a small sample, and we will keep comparing as our agent works with more of the services listed. The methodology page explains how each step is scored if you want to check a grade yourself.

title: Stop Gluing 7 APIs Together: The 5 Tools You Actually Need for Voice AI
author: Vrunda Chauhan
summary: When developers try to build their first voice AI agent, they usually make one big mistake. They connect too many tools. They grab one tool to turn speech into text, another tool for the AI brain, a third tool to generate the voice, a fourth tool for the calendar, and a fifth tool for their customer database. Then they tape it all together with complex webhooks. On paper, it sounds like an amazing setup. Then you test it on a real phone call. You say "Hello," and the line goes completely quiet for three seconds. Just as you start to speak again, the bot finally cuts in and talks over you. In a normal conversation, people only pause for about half a second before speaking. If a computer takes two or three seconds to answer, the caller thinks the call dropped or the system is broken. Building voice agents on our engineering team at EnactOn taught us a simple lesson: great voice agents do not need a dozen different tools. They need a small, clean setup that answers quickly without awkward pauses. Here is how voice AI actually works, the two ways to build it, and the only five tools you need to get started. The Two Ways to Build a Voice Agent Before you connect any extra tools, you must decide how your bot will listen and speak. There are two main ways to do this today: 1. The 3-Step Chain: Caller Speaks -> [Speech-to-Text] -> Text -> [AI Brain] -> Text -> [Voice Maker] -> Bot Speaks 2. Direct Voice AI: Caller Speaks -> [Live Voice AI Model] -> Bot Speaks Method 1: The 3-Step Chain (Listen, Think, Speak) This is the traditional setup most developers start with. You connect three separate tools together: The Ears (Speech-to-Text) : Listens to the caller's voice and types it out as text (using tools like Deepgram or Whisper). The Brain (The AI Model) : Reads the text and decides what to say back (using models like GPT-4o mini or Claude Haiku). The Voice (Text-to-Speech) : Takes the AI's written reply and reads it out loud (using tools like Cartesia or ElevenLabs). This setup gives you total control. You can check the text, filter bad words, and pick any voice you like. The downside is delay. If the ears take 200 milliseconds, the brain takes 400 milliseconds, and the voice takes 250 milliseconds, the caller is already waiting nearly a second. Add in slow phone networks, and the call starts to feel laggy. Method 2: Direct Voice AI (Listen and Speak Directly) Newer models, like the OpenAI Realtime API or Gemini Live, do not convert sound into text and back again. Instead, the AI listens to the audio directly and speaks right back, just like a person on the phone. This cuts the delay in half. The bot can answer in less than half a second. It sounds more natural, and it stops talking the moment the caller interrupts it. The trade-off? Direct voice models cost more to run. When looking at the real cost to build an AI agent , paying for live audio minutes can add up quickly if your bot handles thousands of calls. Once you pick your voice engine, you only need five types of tools to make it useful. 1. The Voice Platform (The Engine) Writing your own code to manage live audio and detect when a person stops talking is very hard. Voice platforms handle this difficult work for you. Popular Tools LiveKit : Great if you are a programmer who wants full control and wants to write your own agent code in Python or Node.js. Vapi and Retell AI : Great if you want a ready-made platform that connects phone numbers, AI brains, and voices in a simple dashboard. OpenAI Realtime & Gemini Live : Foundation-level engines that stream audio directly back and forth. Simple Tip Make sure your bot is not too quick to interrupt. If the bot jumps in every time the caller clears their throat or takes a breath, the call feels stressful. Give the caller about half a second of silence before the bot starts talking. 2. The Phone Line (Telephony) An AI bot running inside your web browser is fun for testing, but a real business needs it to answer normal phone calls. Popular Tools Twilio : The most popular phone service on the internet. It gives your bot real phone numbers and streams live audio directly to your server. Telnyx : A developer-friendly phone service that offers fast connections and low rates for busy phone systems. Simple Tip Do not send phone audio through slow website links. Phone calls need a direct, live stream so words flow back and forth smoothly without cutting out. 3. Customer Memory (CRM) If your bot cannot remember who is calling, it cannot be very helpful. Connecting your bot to a customer database gives it a memory. Popular Tools HubSpot and Salesforce : Well-known systems where businesses store customer names, emails, and past purchases. GoHighLevel : A popular system used by local businesses and clinics to track new leads and messages. Simple Tip Never make the caller wait while the bot searches a big database. If the bot pauses to look up a customer in the middle of a sentence, the caller will hear awkward silence. Instead, look up the person's phone number before answering the call. That way, the bot can say "Hi Alex, thanks for calling back!" on ring one. 4. The Calendar (Scheduling) One of the most useful jobs for a voice bot is booking appointments. But you should never let an AI guess what times are open. Popular Tools Cal.com : A developer-friendly tool for checking open calendar times. Calendly : A widely used booking app that connects directly to Google and Outlook calendars. Google Calendar API : A direct way to check open spots with simple code. Simple Tip Let the AI speak in friendly, everyday language, but let the calendar tool check the actual open dates. That way, your bot will never double-book an appointment by mistake. 5. The Helper Robot (Automation) When a call ends, there are always chores to finish. You might need to send a confirmation text message, update customer notes, or notify your team. Call Ends │ ├──> Write Short Summary │ └──> Trigger Background Chores ├──> Send Text Confirmation to Caller ├──> Update Status in CRM └──> Send Alert to Team in Slack Popular Tools n8n : A powerful automation tool. Running self-hosted n8n workflow automation lets you handle tasks on your own servers without paying extra fees for every single run. Make.com : A friendly visual tool that connects different apps using drag-and-drop steps. Simple Webhooks : Small cloud functions that send data directly from one app to another. Simple Tip Run these chores after the phone call hangs up. Using event-driven ai automation workflows in the background keeps your phone line clear and super fast. Three Simple Rules for a Better Voice Bot Picking your five tools gets your bot working. Following these three simple rules keeps it helpful and polite: 1. Fill Awkward Silences If your bot has to check a slow system, make it say something like "Give me just a second while I check that for you." This lets the caller know the call did not drop. 2. Always Offer a Way to Reach a Human An AI bot should never trap an unhappy customer. If the caller gets frustrated or asks to speak with a person, transfer the call to a real human right away. 3. Keep Private Information Safe Phone calls often involve names, addresses, and phone numbers. Always protect customer data and never store secret passwords in open files. Summary: Keep Your Stack Simple A great voice AI agent is not the one with twenty different tools glued together. It is the one that answers fast, listens carefully, and gets the job done without keeping the caller waiting. Start with a small setup, test your speed on a real phone call, and only add new tools when you really need them. What tools are you using for your voice bot right now? Drop a comment below and share your stack!

title: How Social Media Cookies Fire on Your Site, and How to Gate Them Behind Consent
author: Flora Wilson
summary: Most developers add a Meta Pixel or LinkedIn Insight Tag by pasting a snippet into the page <head> . From then on, the script runs on every page load, which is how social media cookies track visitors before anyone has touched the consent banner. What actually gets set Meta's developer documentation says that when first-party cookies are on, the Pixel saves a unique browser ID to _fbp on your domain. If the visitor came from an ad, the fbclid value is stored in _fbc . LinkedIn's Insight Tag uses UserMatchHistory on .linkedin.com to sync IDs for ad targeting. The first-party detail catches people out. _fbp lives on your domain, yet it serves Meta's advertising, so it still needs consent. Why the site owner is responsible In Fashion ID (C-40/17), the Court of Justice of the EU held that a site embedding Facebook's Like button is a joint controller for collecting and sending visitor data to Facebook, starting from page load. Gating the scripts Remove hardcoded pixel snippets that run before your consent banner. Load them through a consent manager, or Google Tag Manager with consent checks. Reject all in a clean session, then confirm there is no _fbp cookie and no request to facebook.com/tr . Accept, and confirm the pixel fires once. Letting Seers do the gating Wiring this up tag by tag gets tedious. The Seers consent platform scans your site, sorts every cookie and script into a category, and blocks it in real time until the visitor consents. Google Consent Mode v2, Microsoft Consent Mode and IAB TCF v2.2 switch on with one toggle, and there are plugins for WordPress, Shopify, Magento and Drupal. Where server-side fits A server container cuts the scripts running in the browser and gives you one place to apply consent rules. Seers server-side tagging syncs consent with each event and forwards it to Meta's Conversions API, LinkedIn's Conversion API and TikTok's Events API.

title: A security scan says your AI-built app is safe. Does sign-up actually work?
author: VibeTierList
summary: A wave of free scanners for AI-built apps will grade your live URL in under a minute. They're useful. But read their own pages and they're mostly answering one question: what can a stranger grab without logging in? Whether your app actually works for a real user is a different test. Two different questions Security scan: "What can a stranger take?" It reads what your site sends to any browser and makes a few harmless requests: keys in the JavaScript, database tables open to the public key, downloadable .env or .git files, API routes that answer without login, security headers. Logged out, no writes. Functional test: "Does it work for a user?" It uses the app the way a customer would: sign up, log in, create and edit data, tap through it on a phone, log out. It finds the broken button, the stuck sign-up and the page that crashes on an emoji. It can't see a secret key sitting in your code. A security scan can give an A to an app whose sign-up is broken, and a functional test can pass an app that leaks a key. You need both. What five scanners say they check On 20 Oct 2026 we read the pages of five scanners aimed at vibe-coded apps: PreflightVibe, PreflightX, Prodable, Shippable and SafeWeave. This compares methods only (what each page says), not quality. We haven't run them on a test app, and none of them paid us. They overlap heavily on secrets and open data : keys in shipped code, Supabase/Firebase tables or buckets readable without login, API routes that answer without a session. Good, because those leaks expose everyone at once. None of their pages says it tests sign-up, saving data or the phone layout. The ones that say whether they log in say they don't. PreflightVibe is the most direct: it says it can't test what one user can see of another user's data, and tells you to do a two-account test yourself. Full matrix (13 questions × 6 tools, with prices as listed and links to each source page): Security scan vs functional test . Disclosure: we run one of the tools in that matrix (a free functional "Scan my app" beta). It has the same blind spot: it never logs in and blocks every write, and it doesn't look for keys or open tables. What our hands-on test found that no logged-out scan can see On 16 Oct 2026 we built the same multi-user to-do app with Lovable, Bolt, Base44 and v0 on free plans (one run each) and tested every app by hand with real accounts. The problems we found: Buttons that only exist for a mouse (Bolt). Edit and delete appeared only on hover, so on a phone they were invisible. Nothing leaked, so a security check has nothing to find. New users stuck at sign-up (Base44). A new user who closed the email-code page found no way to enter or resend the code from the login screen. You only see this by signing up, closing the tab and coming back. Logging out didn't end the session (Base44). The old access token still worked on the server after logout. A security bug, but a logged-out scan never holds a token to replay. Very short passwords accepted (Lovable). 6-character passwords went through. Finding it means actually creating an account. None of these was a leaked key or an open table. And on the check that matters most, all four apps passed: a second user couldn't see or change the first user's data. That's one run of a simple app, not a promise about yours. What to run before you launch One outside security scan on your live URL, for secret keys, tables readable with your public key and exposed files. Fix anything critical first. A functional pass over your pages: phone layout, buttons, junk input in forms, console and network errors. The logged-in checks, by hand: sign up as a brand-new user (badly), log out and replay the old session, and the two-account test (about 10 minutes with two browser windows). Again after every big change. Each new prompt to your AI builder can quietly undo a fix. The step-by-step version, with a receipt for each step where we have one: 12-step pre-launch checklist for AI-built apps . Originally published on VibeTierList , where we test AI app builders on the same task and publish the receipts. Paying never changes a ranking.

title: AI Production / MLOps
author: Rhuturaj Takle
summary: AI Production / MLOps A deep-dive walkthrough of taking AI applications from a working prototype to a reliable production service on .NET and Azure — covering model deployment patterns, model versioning and registries, model monitoring and drift, CI/CD for AI applications (including evaluation gates), Azure AI services and gateways, Dockerized AI applications, Kubernetes AI workloads, model and response caching, scaling inference, and GPU vs. CPU trade-offs, plus a production-readiness checklist. Table of Contents Introduction Model Deployment Model Versioning Model Monitoring CI/CD for AI Applications Azure AI Services Dockerized AI Applications Kubernetes AI Workloads Model Caching Scaling Inference GPU vs. CPU Considerations Putting It Together Production Readiness Checklist Common Pitfalls Quick Reference Table Conclusion Introduction A prototype proves an idea works once, on your machine, with the inputs you chose. Production means it works every time, for every user, at 3 a.m., under load, after the model provider changes something, with a bill you can predict and a rollback you can trust. The distance between those two states is the subject of MLOps — the discipline of applying DevOps practice (automation, versioning, testing, monitoring, repeatable deployment) to machine learning — and its newer cousin LLMOps , which adapts those practices to applications built on large language models, where "the model" is often someone else's service and the things you ship are prompts, retrieval indexes, tools, and configuration. Two worlds, one discipline: HOSTED-MODEL APPS (LLMOps) You call a managed model (Azure OpenAI and similar). You ship: application code, prompts, retrieval indexes, tool definitions, and configuration. You operate: quotas, gateways, evaluation gates, cost, model-version pinning, provider changes. SELF-HOSTED MODELS (classic MLOps) You run the model: ONNX/ML.NET models in your process, or model servers in containers on CPU/GPU nodes. You ship and operate all of the above PLUS model artifacts, container images, GPU capacity, scaling, and model drift. Most real systems are a mix — a hosted LLM for generation, a self-hosted embedding or vision model, a managed search index — so this guide covers both. The production concerns repeat across both worlds, and they form the sections below: deploy safely, version everything, monitor quality and drift, automate delivery with evaluation gates, package into containers, orchestrate on Kubernetes, cache aggressively and safely, scale to demand, and choose hardware deliberately. It builds directly on earlier guides in this series — AI Observability (what to measure), AI Security (what to lock down), Computer Vision with .NET (serving ONNX models), Microsoft.Extensions.AI (the client abstraction), and RAG (indexes and evaluation) — and focuses on what is specific to running these systems in production. A note on specifics. Azure product names, deployment types, SKUs, quotas, and policy names; Kubernetes operators; GitHub Actions versions; and container base images change frequently. The architecture and principles are the durable part. Verify product-specific details (names, limits, prices, API versions) against current documentation, and treat YAML, Bicep, and policy snippets as illustrative templates to adapt. Model names and numbers in examples are placeholders. 1. Model Deployment What "deploying a model" means depends on where it runs MANAGED MODEL ENDPOINT A provider hosts the model; you create a "deployment" and call it (Azure OpenAI deployments, Azure AI Foundry model deployments, other hosted APIs). + No GPUs to manage, fastest path, provider handles scaling. - Quotas, per-token cost, provider-driven model lifecycle, data leaves your boundary (unless private networking/terms suffice). IN-PROCESS MODEL The model is loaded inside your app: ONNX Runtime or ML.NET in an ASP.NET Core service (classifiers, detectors, embedding models, small LMs). + Lowest latency, no network hop, simplest topology, scales with the app. - Memory per replica, startup time, CPU/GPU contention with the app, tied to app release cadence. SEPARATE MODEL SERVICE A dedicated inference service over HTTP/gRPC (your own container, NVIDIA Triton, vLLM for LLMs, KServe, Azure ML managed online endpoints, Ollama for development). + Independent scaling, GPU isolation, multiple clients, model updates decoupled from the app. - Another service to operate, network latency, more moving parts. SERVERLESS / SCALE-TO-ZERO Azure Container Apps (including serverless GPU workload profiles) or Functions with a model. + Pay only when used, good for spiky or low traffic. - Cold starts (model load!), GPU availability, limits on size and duration. EDGE / ON-DEVICE Models shipped to devices or local servers (ONNX Runtime, DirectML, NPUs). + Offline, private, no per-call cost. - Update distribution, device variability, no central monitoring unless you build it. Decision shortcuts General LLM, no special data-residency or custom-model needs -> managed endpoint (Azure OpenAI) A small model (classifier, detector, embedder) with tight latency -> in-process ONNX/ML.NET A big or GPU-hungry model shared by several apps -> separate model service on GPU nodes (AKS / Azure ML / Container Apps GPU) Occasional, bursty batch jobs -> scale-to-zero jobs or serverless; batch APIs for hosted models Strict offline/privacy requirements -> self-hosted open-weight model or on-device Deploying managed models as code Treat a model deployment like any other infrastructure: declared in code, reviewed, and pinned. // An Azure OpenAI deployment declared as infrastructure (illustrative — verify the API version, model name, version, SKU names, and capacity units) resource chatDeployment 'Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments@2024-10-01' = { parent: openAiAccount name: 'chat-prod' // the deployment name your app uses (the app never hard-codes the underlying model name) sku: { name: 'Standard' // pay-per-token; provisioned throughput SKUs exist for predictable latency at steady load capacity: 100 // quota units (thousands of tokens per minute) } properties: { model: { format: 'OpenAI', name: 'gpt-4o-mini', version: '2024-07-18' } versionUpgradeOption: 'NoAutoUpgrade' // PIN the model version: upgrades happen when YOU choose, after evaluation raiPolicyName: 'prod-content-policy' // server-side content filter policy } } Why this matters: - PINNED VERSION: a silent upgrade can change behavior (and quality) under you. Pin, evaluate the new version in a parallel deployment, then switch. - DEPLOYMENT NAMES decouple code from model names: moving "chat-prod" to a new model is an infrastructure change, not a code deploy. - ENVIRONMENT PARITY: dev/test/prod deployments created from the same template. - SERVER-SIDE POLICY: content filters and quotas set where callers can't weaken them (see AI Security, Section 12). Deploying self-hosted models PACKAGE Export to a portable format (ONNX from PyTorch/TensorFlow; an ML.NET model .zip), optimize and optionally quantize, and record a manifest (Section 2). STORE Put artifacts in a model registry or versioned blob storage (not in source control for large files, not only inside a container image). LOAD At startup, fetch the model, verify its checksum, create ONE inference session, and run a warm-up inference. GATE Don't accept traffic until the model is loaded and warm: readiness probes (below). A pod that serves requests while still loading just returns errors. ROLL OUT Blue/green, canary, or shadow — compare the new model to the old on real traffic before cutting over (Section 3). ONNX Runtime session configuration using Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime ; var options = new SessionOptions { GraphOptimizationLevel = GraphOptimizationLevel . ORT_ENABLE_ALL , // graph-level optimizations (operator fusion, constant folding) IntraOpNumThreads = int . Parse ( Environment . GetEnvironmentVariable ( "ORT_INTRA_OP_THREADS" ) ?? "4" ), // match the container's CPU limit — don't oversubscribe ExecutionMode = ExecutionMode . ORT_SEQUENTIAL , }; // GPU (requires the Microsoft.ML.OnnxRuntime.Gpu package, plus matching CUDA/cuDNN libraries in the image): // options.AppendExecutionProvider_CUDA(deviceId: 0); var session = new InferenceSession ( modelPath , options ); // create ONCE per process; Run() is safe to call concurrently Readiness: don't take traffic until the model is warm public sealed class ModelState { public volatile bool Ready ; } public sealed class ModelLoader ( ModelState state , ObjectDetector detector , ILogger < ModelLoader > log ) : BackgroundService { protected override Task ExecuteAsync ( CancellationToken stoppingToken ) { // Loading and a dummy inference happen at startup, off the request path detector . WarmUp (); // run a few inferences on a synthetic image to initialize kernels and allocators state . Ready = true ; log . LogInformation ( "Model loaded and warm" ); return Task . CompletedTask ; } } public sealed class ModelReadyCheck ( ModelState state ) : IHealthCheck { public Task < HealthCheckResult > CheckHealthAsync ( HealthCheckContext context , CancellationToken ct = default ) => Task . FromResult ( state . Ready ? HealthCheckResult . Healthy () : HealthCheckResult . Unhealthy ( "Model not ready" )); } builder . Services . AddSingleton < ModelState >(); builder . Services . AddHostedService < ModelLoader >(); builder . Services . AddHealthChecks (). AddCheck < ModelReadyCheck >( "model" , tags : [ "ready" ]); app . MapHealthChecks ( "/health/ready" , new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = c => c . Tags . Contains ( "ready" ) }); // Kubernetes readiness probe app . MapHealthChecks ( "/health/live" , new HealthCheckOptions { Predicate = _ => false }); // liveness: "the process is up" — does NOT depend on the model (Keep liveness independent of the model, or a slow model load gets the pod killed in a restart loop.) Release strategies for models BLUE/GREEN Run old and new side by side; switch traffic at once; instant rollback by switching back. Doubles capacity during the switch. CANARY Send a small share (1%, 5%, 25%...) to the new version, watch metrics (quality, latency, errors, cost), and expand or roll back automatically. SHADOW Mirror real traffic to the new version, discard its responses, and compare offline (quality, cost, latency). Zero user risk; best for validating a new model or prompt. A/B TEST Randomly split users between versions and compare outcomes (feedback, task success). Needs enough traffic and a clear success metric. ROLLING Replace replicas gradually (Kubernetes default) — fine for app code, but for models make sure old and new replicas can coexist and produce compatible outputs. ALWAYS Keep the previous version deployable, record which version served each request (trace attribute), and define rollback criteria BEFORE the rollout. 2. Model Versioning Version everything that changes behavior In classic software, the code version identifies behavior. In AI systems, behavior is the product of many artifacts, any of which can change independently — so every one needs a version, and every request should record which versions served it. MODEL WEIGHTS The ONNX file, ML.NET .zip, or fine-tuned checkpoint (and, for hosted models, the provider's model + version string) TOKENIZER / VOCAB / LABELS Must match the weights exactly — a tokenizer mismatch silently destroys accuracy PREPROCESSING / POSTPROCESSING CONFIG Input size, normalization, thresholds, NMS settings, label maps PROMPTS System prompts, templates, few-shot examples, judge rubrics (a prompt change is a behavior change) RETRIEVAL INDEX Index contents version, chunking strategy, and the EMBEDDING MODEL used (changing the embedding model invalidates every stored vector) TOOL DEFINITIONS Names, descriptions, schemas, and permissions EVALUATION SETS The golden set and its grading rubrics — so scores are comparable over time INFRASTRUCTURE / CONFIG Deployment templates, quotas, content-filter policies, price tables DATA (for training) The dataset version, to make training reproducible CODE Application and pipeline code (git commit) A model manifest: identity, lineage, and integrity public record ModelManifest ( string Name , // "vision-detector" string Version , // semantic version: bump MAJOR when outputs/labels/contract change, MINOR for retrains with the same contract, PATCH for fixes string Sha256 , // checksum of the model artifact — verified at load time string InputSpec , // "rgb 640x640 float32 0..1 NCHW, letterboxed" string [] Labels , string TrainingDataVersion , // lineage: which data string GitCommit , // lineage: which code DateTimeOffset TrainedAt , Dictionary < string , double > EvalMetrics ); // what it scored when it was registered (mAP, accuracy, etc.) public static class ModelVerifier { // Refuse to load an artifact whose checksum doesn't match its manifest — protects against corruption, wrong files, and tampering public static async Task VerifyAsync ( string modelPath , ModelManifest manifest ) { await using FileStream stream = File . OpenRead ( modelPath ); byte [] hash = await SHA256 . HashDataAsync ( stream ); if (! Convert . ToHexString ( hash ). Equals ( manifest . Sha256 , StringComparison . OrdinalIgnoreCase )) throw new InvalidOperationException ( $"Model { manifest . Name } @ { manifest . Options: Azure Machine Learning model registry · MLflow Model Registry · Hugging Face Hub (private repos) · OCI registries (artifacts in Azure Container Registry) · versioned Blob Storage with a manifest. PRINCIPLES IMMUTABLE A published version is never overwritten. A fix is a NEW version. LINEAGE Each version records its training data version, code commit, hyperparameters, and evaluation metrics. PROMOTION dev -> staging -> production via stages, aliases, or tags (for example "champion" and "challenger"), gated by evaluation and approval — and audited. ROLLBACK Re-pointing the production alias to the previous version is a one-line, instant operation. ACCESS CONTROL Who can register, promote, and read models — models are valuable and, if poisoned, dangerous (see AI Security, Section 12). Hosted models: version pinning and lifecycle Providers retire model versions on a published schedule, and some "latest" aliases move without notice. For hosted models: PIN the version in your deployment (see the Bicep above); never rely on an unpinned alias for a production workload that you've evaluated. TRACK RETIREMENT DATES for every model you use and put the migration on your calendar well ahead of time. MIGRATE DELIBERATELY: stand up the new version as a parallel deployment, run your evaluation suite against it, shadow/canary it, then switch — treat it as a release, not a config tweak. RECORD the actual model/version from each response (response.ModelId) on traces and logs so a provider-side change is visible (see AI Observability, Section 8). Prompts and indexes are versioned artifacts too PROMPTS Files in source control (prompts/support-answer/v12.md), loaded by name and version, changed through pull requests with evaluation results attached. Tag every trace with the prompt name and version. Support deploying a prompt change independently of code when needed — but through the same review, evaluation, and rollout discipline. INDEXES Build a NEW index for any change to chunking, the embedding model, or the schema; validate it with the golden set; then switch an ALIAS or configuration pointer (blue/green for indexes). Keep the old index until the new one is proven. Store the embedding model name and index version in each record and in the index metadata. COMPATIBILITY Keep a matrix of which model version works with which tokenizer, preprocessing, labels, prompt version, and downstream consumers. A model that adds a class or changes an output shape is a breaking change for everything that consumes it — treat it as a MAJOR version. 3. Model Monitoring The AI Observability guide covers instrumenting logs, metrics, traces, cost, and RAG quality in depth. This section covers what is specific to models in production : detecting that the world has moved out from under them. Why models decay DATA DRIFT The distribution of inputs changes (new customer segment, a new camera, a new product line, seasonal language, a different mix of languages). CONCEPT DRIFT The relationship between inputs and the right answer changes (fraud tactics evolve, "good" customer behavior changes, a policy changes the labels). PREDICTION DRIFT The distribution of outputs shifts (the classifier suddenly predicts one class far more often) — often the earliest visible symptom. UPSTREAM CHANGE A feature pipeline, tokenizer, data source, or the provider's model changes without notice. CORPUS CHANGE (RAG) The documents change or the index is rebuilt; retrieval quality shifts with them. A model that was excellent at launch quietly gets worse. Without monitoring, you learn about it from customers. Layers of model monitoring 1. SYSTEM HEALTH Availability, error classes, latency, throughput, GPU/CPU/memory, queue depth (Section 9 and AI Observability). 2. INPUT / DATA QUALITY Schema and range checks, missing values, new categories, language mix, image size and format distribution, text-length distribution. 3. DATA DRIFT Statistical comparison of live input distributions against a reference (the training or validation data, or a recent healthy window). 4. PREDICTION DRIFT Distribution of predicted classes, scores, and confidence over time; rising share of low-confidence or "unknown" outputs. 5. MODEL PERFORMANCE Actual accuracy/precision/recall/F1 (or task success) — which requires ground truth, often delayed (below). 6. BUSINESS IMPACT The KPI the model exists to move: conversion, fraud caught, handling time, deflection, defect escape rate. Getting ground truth: the hard part Performance metrics need labels, and in production labels arrive late, partially, or never. DELAYED LABELS Outcomes known later (a loan defaults in 12 months, a return occurs in 30 days). Monitor leading indicators (drift, confidence) in the meantime, then backfill performance. HUMAN REVIEW Route a sample (and all low-confidence cases) to reviewers; their decisions are labeled data and a live accuracy estimate. USER FEEDBACK Corrections, overrides, thumbs, escalations — biased and sparse, but valuable signals. CANARY SETS A fixed labeled set re-scored on a schedule detects model/pipeline regressions even without fresh labels. PROXY METRICS Confidence distributions, agreement between the model and a stronger offline model, and consistency checks. Platforms such as Azure Machine Learning model monitoring and open-source libraries (for example Evidently, a Python library) can compute these; you can also run them from .NET jobs. Compute drift on a schedule (hourly/daily windows), emit the scores as metrics, and alert on thresholds. Monitoring hosted LLM applications You can't observe weights or training data, so monitor behavior: MODEL VERSION Alert when response.ModelId changes (provider update) — record it on every trace. CANARY GOLDEN SET Run it on a schedule against production configuration; alert on score drops (see AI Observability, Section 8). OUTPUT STATISTICS Length, refusal rate, format-failure rate, finish-reason mix, language, sentiment — sudden shifts mean something changed. INPUT STATISTICS Prompt length, language mix, topic clusters, new intents. QUALITY SAMPLING Sampled LLM-judge scores and user feedback by prompt/model/index version. COST AND LATENCY Tokens per request, cost per outcome, TTFT percentiles. From alert to action: retraining and rollback TRIGGERS Drift above threshold · performance below SLO · new data volume · schedule (for example quarterly) · a significant upstream or business change. RESPONSE Investigate (is it real drift or a pipeline bug?) -> retrain or fine-tune on fresh data, or update prompts/index -> evaluate against the golden set AND recent real data -> shadow/canary -> promote with approval -> monitor. Rollback to the previous version if the new one underperforms. AUTOMATION Automate the pipeline (data -> train -> evaluate -> register), but keep a HUMAN approval gate before promotion to production for anything consequential. GUARDRAIL Beware feedback loops: if model predictions influence the data you later train on (recommendations shape clicks), monitor for self-reinforcing bias. 4. CI/CD for AI Applications What's different about CI/CD for AI A conventional pipeline asks "does the code compile and do the tests pass?" An AI pipeline must also ask "is the behavior still good?" — and that answer is statistical, depends on external models, and costs money to compute. So an AI pipeline adds evaluation gates alongside unit tests, treats prompts, models, and indexes as deployable artifacts, and often separates code deployment from model/prompt promotion. CODE CHANGE build · unit tests (fake chat client) · static analysis · dependency + secret scanning · container build + scan · deploy · smoke test PROMPT CHANGE lint · EVALUATION against the golden set · security (injection) suite · cost/latency check · review · promote · canary MODEL CHANGE registry registration · EVALUATION on held-out + recent data · performance benchmark (latency/throughput on target hardware) · shadow/canary · promote with approval INDEX CHANGE build new index · retrieval evaluation (Recall@k, MRR) · switch alias · monitor · keep the old index for rollback INFRA CHANGE IaC plan/what-if · policy checks · deploy to staging · verify quotas and content-filter policy The test pyramid for AI applications UNIT TESTS (fast, deterministic, free) Business logic, prompt assembly, history trimming, tool wiring and authorization, validators, parsers — against a FAKE IChatClient (see Microsoft.Extensions.AI, Section 10). Run on every commit. INTEGRATION TESTS Real vector store/database in a container (Testcontainers), real HTTP pipeline, still a fake or recorded model. Verifies plumbing. EVALUATION TESTS (slower, statistical, costs money) The golden set run against the REAL model/prompt/index: retrieval metrics, judged faithfulness, citation validity, task success, refusal behavior, cost and latency. Repeat each case several times (non-determinism). Compare to a baseline. Run when prompts, models, retrieval, or tools change — not necessarily on every commit. SECURITY TESTS The adversarial suite: injection, exfiltration, cross-tenant access, tool misuse (see AI Security, Section 14). A release gate. LOAD / PERFORMANCE TESTS Throughput, latency percentiles, saturation, and cost at target traffic — on production-like hardware. SMOKE / SYNTHETIC CHECKS After deploy and continuously in production: a handful of real end-to-end requests. RUN dotnet publish src/VisionApi/VisionApi.csproj -c Release -o /app/publish --no-restore /p:UseAppHost = false # ---- runtime stage ---- FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:9.0 AS runtime WORKDIR /app COPY --from=build /app/publish . # The model is NOT baked into the image: it is mounted or fetched at startup (see below) ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080 \ MODEL_PATH=/models/model.onnx \ ORT_INTRA_OP_THREADS=4 EXPOSE 8080 USER $APP_UID # run as non-root (the base image defines APP_UID) ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "VisionApi.dll"] (Use the image tag matching your target .NET version, and pin base images by digest in production for reproducible builds.) Where should the model live? BAKED INTO THE IMAGE + Self-contained, simplest, versioned together with the app, fast startup (no download). - Huge images (slow pulls and pushes, registry cost), every model update rebuilds and redeploys the image, secrets/licensing concerns if the model is sensitive. Good for: small models (tens of MB) that change rarely. MOUNTED VOLUME + Decouples model from image; many pods can share a read-only volume (Azure Files / Blob CSI); update the model without rebuilding. - Volume performance and availability become dependencies; versioning is a convention you must enforce. DOWNLOADED AT STARTUP + Image stays small; the model version comes from configuration; works with a registry or blob storage and checksum verification (Section 2). (INIT CONTAINER OR APP) - Cold start includes the download — mitigate with node-local caching, an init container, and a startup probe that waits for readiness. Good for: large or frequently updated models. The usual choice for GPU and LLM-scale artifacts. RULE OF THUMB Small + stable: bake in. Large or changing: fetch/mount, verify the checksum, cache on the node. Base images and native dependencies GLIBC vs. MUSL Native ML libraries (ONNX Runtime, OpenCV, CUDA) are built for glibc. Alpine's musl libc often breaks them or lacks official builds. Prefer Debian/Ubuntu-based .NET images for AI workloads. CHISELED IMAGES Minimal, non-root, shell-less Ubuntu images shrink size and attack surface — but they omit packages some native libraries need. Test thoroughly before adopting. GPU IMAGES Use an NVIDIA CUDA runtime base (with cuDNN) matching the CUDA/cuDNN versions your ONNX Runtime GPU package requires, install the .NET runtime on top (or copy it in), and run with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit (--gpus all locally; the device plugin in Kubernetes). A version mismatch is the classic cause of silent fallback to CPU (Section 10). OPENCV Include the matching OpenCvSharp runtime package for your OS and any required system libraries; test in the final image, not on your dev machine. KEEP IT SMALL Multi-stage builds; no SDK in the runtime image; a .dockerignore; don't copy test data or model files you don't need. Container hygiene for AI services NON-ROOT Run as an unprivileged user; read-only root filesystem where possible; drop capabilities. NO SECRETS IN IMAGES Inject at runtime (environment from Key Vault, mounted secrets, workload identity). Images are copied around and scanned; assume they leak. SCAN, SBOM, SIGN Vulnerability-scan (for example Trivy or Defender for Containers), produce an SBOM, sign images, and verify signatures at admission. PIN EVERYTHING Base image digests, package versions, model checksums. RESOURCE AWARENESS .NET respects container CPU and memory limits; set ONNX Runtime thread counts from the CPU limit, and size memory for the model plus request buffers (large image decodes, long prompts). GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN Handle SIGTERM: stop accepting new work, let in-flight inference finish (HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout), then exit. Align with Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds. LOGS TO STDOUT Structured logs and OpenTelemetry export — no local log files. HEALTH ENDPOINTS /health/live (process up) and /health/ready (model loaded) for orchestrators (Section 1). Each saves a different cost — and each has distinct staleness and security risks. The kinds of caching 1. RESPONSE CACHE (EXACT) Same inputs -> stored output. Skips the model entirely. 2. SEMANTIC CACHE "Similar enough" questions share a stored answer, matched by embedding similarity. 3. PROVIDER PROMPT CACHE The provider discounts and speeds up requests that begin with a recently processed prompt prefix. 4. EMBEDDING CACHE Content hash -> vector. Avoids re-embedding unchanged text or repeated queries. 5. KV CACHE (self-hosted LLMs) The attention key/value cache inside the inference server, including prefix caching across requests. 6. MODEL ARTIFACT CACHE Model files cached on nodes/volumes so pods don't re-download them; image layers cached; warm pools of loaded models. 7. IN-PROCESS MODEL CACHE The loaded model session held in memory (singleton), or an LRU of several models when you serve many. 8. PREDICTION CACHE For deterministic classical models: input features -> prediction. Provider prompt caching: arrange prompts to benefit Providers can automatically discount and speed up requests whose beginning matches a recently processed prompt (typically applying above a minimum prompt length — check current thresholds and discounts). TO BENEFIT: - Put STATIC content FIRST: system prompt, instructions, tool definitions, reference documents. Put VARIABLE content LAST: the user's question, retrieved passages that change per request. - Keep the static prefix BYTE-IDENTICAL across requests (no timestamps, request IDs, or reordered tools at the top). - Track the cached-token share (see AI Observability, Section 3): a drop means your prefix changed. Scaling Inference Start with the arithmetic LITTLE'S LAW: concurrency = throughput x latency A service handling 50 requests/second at 0.4 s per request has ~20 requests in flight on average. If one replica can handle 5 concurrent requests before latency degrades, you need ~4 replicas at average load — plus headroom for peaks (commonly 30-50%) and for losing a replica. For LLM calls to a hosted provider, also compute TOKEN throughput: requests/s x (input + output tokens) must fit your tokens-per-minute quota. Always LOAD TEST: measure latency percentiles at increasing load on production-like hardware, find the knee where latency climbs, and set capacity and autoscaling targets below it. Levers for scaling, in rough order of leverage 1. DON'T DO THE WORK Caching (Section 8), deduplication, cheaper routing — the fastest request is the one you skip. 2. MAKE EACH REQUEST CHEAPER Smaller or distilled models, quantization (FP16/INT8), shorter prompts and outputs, graph optimization, efficient runtimes (ONNX Runtime, TensorRT, OpenVINO, DirectML). 3. BATCH Process several requests per model invocation — raises throughput substantially on GPUs (and helps CPUs), at a latency cost (below). 4. SCALE OUT More stateless replicas behind a load balancer, autoscaled on the right signals (Section 7). 5. SCALE UP Bigger or faster hardware (more cores, a GPU, a larger GPU) when one model invocation itself is the bottleneck. 6. SHIFT WORK OFF THE REQUEST PATH Queues and background workers for anything users aren't waiting on. Stateless replicas and load balancing Inference services should be stateless (conversation and cache state live in external stores) so any replica can serve any request and replicas can be added or removed freely. LOAD BALANCING GOTCHA: inference request durations vary enormously (a 50-token answer vs. a 2,000-token answer). Plain round-robin can pile long requests on one replica. Prefer least-connections or queue-aware balancing, and cap per-replica concurrency so overload is rejected quickly instead of queueing indefinitely. Optimizing the model itself QUANTIZATION Reduce numeric precision (FP32 -> FP16 -> INT8, and lower for LLMs) to cut memory and increase speed, usually with a small accuracy cost — always re-evaluate quality after quantizing. DISTILLATION Train a small "student" model to mimic a large "teacher" — often the best accuracy-per-cost for a specific task. PRUNING / SMALLER ARCHITECTURES Remove redundancy or pick a more efficient architecture for the task. GRAPH OPTIMIZATION ONNX Runtime operator fusion and constant folding; hardware-specific runtimes (TensorRT for NVIDIA GPUs, OpenVINO for Intel CPUs, DirectML on Windows GPUs/NPUs). SHORTER SEQUENCES Trim prompts and outputs; resize images to the smallest resolution that preserves accuracy. RIGHT-SIZE THE MODEL Use the smallest model that meets the quality bar — then route harder requests to a bigger one (see LLM Application Development, Section 9). Scaling hosted-LLM usage QUOTAS ARE THE CEILING Your throughput is capped by tokens-per-minute and requests-per-minute quotas. Plan capacity from token estimates, not request counts. MULTIPLE DEPLOYMENTS/REGIONS Spread load across several deployments (and regions where data-residency allows) behind a gateway that load-balances, honors Retry-After, and trips circuit breakers on 429s and 5xx. PROVISIONED + STANDARD Reserved (provisioned) capacity for the steady baseline, with pay-as-you-go capacity as burst or fallback. BATCH API FOR OFFLINE WORK Move non-interactive jobs off the real-time quota and onto discounted asynchronous batch processing. RESILIENCE Retries with jittered backoff, timeouts, circuit breakers, and fallbacks (cheaper model, cached answer, degraded feature) — see AI APIs with .NET, Section 10. CLIENT-SIDE LIMITS Bound concurrency and token rates in your app so you degrade gracefully before the provider rejects you (see AI Security, Section 11). Multi-region and failover ACTIVE-ACTIVE OR ACTIVE-PASSIVE across regions for the application, the index, and model endpoints, behind a global load balancer (Azure Front Door/Traffic Manager). Replicate indexes and artifacts; keep model versions and prompts consistent across regions; test failover regularly; and account for data-residency constraints (not every region may be eligible for every tenant). 10. GPU vs. CPU Considerations The decision is about utilization and cost per inference, not raw speed A GPU does a lot of parallel arithmetic quickly, but it is expensive whether or not it is busy. A CPU is slower per operation but cheap, flexible, and everywhere. The right choice depends on model size, traffic shape, latency target, and — above all — how well you can keep the hardware utilized . Where GPUs win LARGE MODELS Transformers, large vision models, and LLMs with many millions or billions of parameters. HIGH, STEADY THROUGHPUT Enough traffic to keep the GPU busy, especially with batching. LATENCY-CRITICAL HEAVY MODELS When a CPU simply can't meet the latency target for the model size. BATCH EMBEDDING / BULK INFERENCE Large offline jobs where throughput per dollar dominates. SELF-HOSTED LLM SERVING Practically requires GPUs (or accelerators) for useful speed at scale. Where CPUs win SMALL MODELS Classical ML, gradient-boosted trees, small neural nets, small embedding/classification models (tens to low hundreds of millions of parameters, quantized). LOW OR BURSTY TRAFFIC An idle GPU burns money; CPU instances scale to zero or run cheaply at low utilization. BATCH SIZE OF ONE, LOW LATENCY Small single-item inferences often run just as fast on CPU (no host-to-device transfer overhead). OPERATIONAL SIMPLICITY No driver/CUDA/image-version matrix, easier scheduling and autoscaling, broader availability. QUANTIZED MODELS INT8/INT4 on modern CPUs (AVX2/AVX-512/VNNI instructions) can be surprisingly fast for the right models. ARM CPUs Often the best price/performance for CPU-bound inference where supported. The binding constraint is often memory, not compute MODEL MEMORY (rule of thumb): parameters x bytes per parameter 7-billion-parameter model: FP16 (2 bytes) ≈ 14 GB; INT8 ≈ 7 GB; 4-bit ≈ 3.5-4 GB — PLUS the KV cache and activations KV CACHE grows with context length and concurrent sequences; for LLM serving it frequently limits concurrency more than the weights do. A model that doesn't fit in GPU memory doesn't run (or must be split across GPUs/offloaded to CPU at a heavy speed penalty). Quantization is therefore both a cost lever and a feasibility lever. For LLM decoding, speed is often limited by memory BANDWIDTH rather than raw compute. A decision table Situation Likely best choice Classical ML (trees, linear models), ML.NET CPU Small classifier/embedder, low-to-moderate traffic CPU (quantized if needed) Object detection at video frame rates GPU Large vision/transformer model, high throughput GPU with batching Bursty or sporadic usage CPU, or serverless/scale-to-zero (GPU only if the model demands it) Self-hosted LLM for many users GPU (right-sized, with a serving stack that batches continuously) Self-hosted small language model, few users, modest speed needs Quantized on CPU may suffice Offline bulk embedding/inference GPU or many CPUs — compare cost per million items; spot capacity helps Edge/desktop devices NPU/integrated GPU via DirectML or vendor runtimes, with a CPU fallback Hosted LLM API Not applicable — you choose a deployment type and quota, not hardware Benchmark on your own model and traffic Don't decide from spec sheets. Measure, for each candidate hardware option (and a few batch sizes): THROUGHPUT items (or tokens) per second at saturation LATENCY p50/p95/p99 at your expected concurrency COST PER 1,000 INFERENCES = instance cost per hour / (throughput per hour / 1000), at realistic UTILIZATION (not 100%) MEMORY peak usage; headroom for your largest inputs QUALITY after quantization or precision changes — re-run your evaluation set Then compare cost per inference at the utilization you will actually achieve. GPU for large/steady; size for memory; verify GPU is actually used Readiness Production checklist SLOs, rollback, quotas, security, cost, runbooks, kill switches Conclusion Production AI is mostly the disciplined application of ideas you already know — versioned artifacts, automated pipelines, gradual rollouts, health probes, autoscaling, monitoring, and rollback — adapted to systems whose behavior is statistical, whose dependencies change without notice, and whose cost scales with usage. The adaptations are what matter: version everything that affects behavior (weights, tokenizers, prompts, indexes, tools, evaluation sets) and stamp each request with those versions; gate releases on evaluation and security tests , not just unit tests, using repeated runs and baselines to handle non-determinism; monitor drift and quality , not just uptime, with canary evaluations that catch the silent provider and data changes nobody announces; and roll out gradually through shadow, canary, and blue/green strategies with rollback criteria defined in advance. On the infrastructure side, the same few themes recur. Gate traffic on readiness , not on process start. Keep model delivery out of the request path (verified downloads, node-local caches, warm capacity). Scale on the right signals (concurrency, queue depth, GPU metrics) and shed load early instead of queueing until everything is slow. Put a gateway in front of hosted models for authentication, token limits, metrics, caching, and failover, and use keyless identity everywhere. Cache aggressively but safely — keyed on everything that changes the answer, scoped by tenant, invalidated on every version change. And choose hardware by cost per inference at the utilization you will really achieve , sizing for memory as well as compute and verifying that the GPU you pay for is actually the one doing the work. Pair those practices with a readiness checklist, rehearsed rollbacks, kill switches, and runbooks, and an AI feature stops being a demo that works until it doesn't and becomes a service your team can change confidently, operate predictably, and afford.
