title: How I Structure a Next.js + NestJS Project for AI Coding Agents
author: Nael M. Awadallah
summary: An AI coding agent can put a working feature in the wrong place. The button works. The endpoint returns 200. TypeScript is happy. But the change also introduces a second API client, copies a billing rule into React, and imports another module's private files. Every local decision looks reasonable. Together, they make the next feature harder. That is the problem I want my project structure to address: make the intended place for a change easier to find than a plausible alternative. Here is the structure I would use for a Next.js frontend and a NestJS backend, with a ticket-management feature as the running example. This is an architectural recommendation, not a benchmark claiming that a folder layout makes agents a certain percentage more accurate. The goal is practical: give both developers and coding agents a clear answer to four questions: Where does this behavior belong? Which other parts may it depend on? What information crosses the API? How do we verify the change? 1. Start with ownership, then choose folders Consider a request: show the outstanding balance on a ticket and let an operator record a payment. Before choosing filenames, I want this ownership map: Concern Owner Ticket card, dialog, loading state Frontend ticket feature HTTP request and query invalidation Frontend ticket API and hooks Permission to record a payment Backend authorization Payment validation and persistence Backend payment collection use case Authoritative balance Backend billing logic API response shape Explicit response DTO The frontend may format a balance. It does not become the authority on whether a payment is valid. This matters because a vague instruction such as “add payment support” leaves architectural decisions hidden inside an implementation task. A small ownership table makes those decisions visible before code is written. 2. Keep the repository map boring For a monorepo, my starting layout would be: apps/ web/ AGENTS.md src/ app/ modules/ components/ui/ lib/ api/ AGENTS.md src/ modules/ common/ docs/ architecture.md decisions/ AGENTS.md The root instructions explain how the applications fit together. Application instructions contain commands and conventions specific to that application. A short architecture document explains ownership and dependency direction. This does not require a monorepo. With separate repositories, I would keep the same internal structure and document the counterpart repository and contract-generation workflow. I would also identify the relevant backend and frontend branches when assigning a task. Moving two repositories into one is not a prerequisite for using an agent well. 3. In Next.js, organize application code by feature Next.js supports several organization strategies. Keeping features outside app/ is a convention I choose, rather than a framework requirement. For a ticket feature: src/modules/tickets/ api/ tickets.api.ts ticket-query-keys.ts components/ ticket-card.tsx payment-dialog.tsx hooks/ use-record-payment.ts pages/ tickets-page.tsx types/ ticket.types.ts index.ts I create a directory when there is something to put in it. A feature with two files does not need six empty folders. The route stays small: // src/app/(dashboard)/tickets/page.tsx import { TicketsPage } from " @/modules/tickets " ; export default function Page () { return < TicketsPage />; } Route-specific responsibilities can stay in app/ : layouts, metadata, route parameters, and route-level data loading. Business UI lives with its feature. When an agent needs to change the payment dialog, the surrounding API call, hook, and types are nearby. It has a useful starting point without needing a global components/ or hooks/ directory to explain the whole application. Make public entry points deliberate My feature entry point exports only what other features need: // src/modules/tickets/index.ts export { TicketsPage } from " ./pages/tickets-page " ; export type { TicketSummary } from " ./types/ticket.types " ; Other features use that public entry point. Files inside the ticket feature can use relative imports. I do not export every helper “just in case.” Each export is another dependency the project may need to support later. There is also a Next.js-specific boundary to preserve: client and server code. A public entry point should not casually mix interactive UI with database access or server-only secrets. When a feature needs both, I use distinct entry points such as client.ts and server.ts , and mark server-only implementation files appropriately. A barrel file is a navigation convention. It is not a security boundary. 4. In NestJS, distinguish a folder from a module A larger ticket feature might look like this: src/modules/tickets/ tickets.module.ts tickets.controller.ts tickets.service.ts dto/ ticket-summary.dto.ts entities/ ticket.entity.ts payment-collection/ payment-collection.controller.ts payment-collection.service.ts dto/ record-payment.dto.ts payment-collection/ groups a cohesive use case. It does not automatically require its own Nest module. Its controller and provider can be registered by TicketsModule . I would introduce another module when it needs a distinct dependency boundary or a responsibility that extends beyond tickets. For example, chat may grow to own messages, participants, unread counts, and realtime delivery. Tickets can be one context chat refers to without owning the entire chat subsystem. Nest modules make dependencies explicit through imports, providers, and exports. My default is to export the smallest service another module actually needs. A focused ticket lookup service can be a better dependency than a service exposing every ticket mutation. I avoid treating direct access to another module's repository as the automatic shortcut. If repository access is intentional, I document who owns the rules that must still apply. The question is: does this responsibility need its own boundary? File count alone does not answer it. 5. Make the API contract carry the meaning The frontend should consume a response designed for the use case, rather than importing an ORM entity. Here is an illustrative response type: type TicketSummary = { id : string ; currency : string ; totalMinor : number | null ; paidMinor : number ; outstandingMinor : number | null ; }; The contract also needs semantics: Money uses integer minor units for the specified currency. In this example, totalMinor: null means the charge is not finalized. outstandingMinor: null means a final outstanding balance is not available. paidMinor represents confirmed payments; refunds and credits need explicitly defined treatment if supported. The backend determines the authoritative outstanding amount. Without those definitions, an agent might turn null into zero and display an unfinished charge as “Paid.” The type checker would accept it. For this example, I would specify the expected responses before implementation: Case Total Paid Outstanding Charge still running null 0 null Final charge, unpaid 6000 0 6000 Partial payment 6000 2000 4000 Fully paid 6000 6000 0 These are example rules, not universal billing rules. A product that supports advance payments needs additional cases. For a growing project, I would generate frontend types from a maintained OpenAPI schema. NestJS provides OpenAPI tooling, but useful generated types still depend on accurate response schemas. Generated types can detect a renamed property. They cannot explain what “finalized” means. That belongs in the contract documentation and behavior tests. 6. Give agents instructions they can act on “Write clean code” leaves almost every decision open. I want instructions like these instead: # Project instructions ## Ownership - apps/web owns presentation and interaction. - apps/api owns authorization, billing, and persistence. - Follow an existing nearby implementation before adding a pattern. ## Boundaries - Import another frontend feature through its public entry point. - Keep server-only code out of client entry points. - Keep ORM entities inside the backend. - Document API changes and regenerate contract types when applicable. ## Scope - Make the smallest cohesive change that satisfies the task. - Avoid unrelated renames and dependency changes. - Surface unresolved business rules before implementing them. ## Verification - Use the commands in the relevant application's AGENTS.md. - Report which checks ran, their results, and any blocked checks. AGENTS.md is an instruction format supported by multiple coding tools. Support and loading behavior vary, so I check the tool's documentation rather than assuming every agent reads every file. For Claude Code, I would use its documented CLAUDE.md mechanism and import the shared guidance where appropriate: @AGENTS.md I would verify that the expected instructions are loaded in the actual working directory. One maintained set of rules is easier to trust than two copies that slowly disagree. Application instructions should include commands that really exist. If the backend uses npm and Jest, those instructions should say so. Example commands pasted from a pnpm project are worse than no commands when they send the agent down the wrong path. 7. Put business decisions somewhere that survives the chat Suppose a ticket costs more the longer a car stays parked. The decision “freeze the charge when retrieval is requested” affects more than one method: The backend needs a finalization point. The API needs to distinguish an ongoing charge from a finalized one. The UI needs different states. Cancellation and a second retrieval request need defined behavior. Tests need to preserve the decision. I would record the rule in a short decision document: # Billing finalization Status: accepted for this example Decision: Finalize the charge when retrieval is requested. Consequences: - Waiting for retrieval does not increase the finalized charge. - A repeated request must not finalize the same charge twice. Unresolved: - Whether cancellation reopens billing. - Which pricing policy applies to a later request. The unresolved section is useful. It gives the agent a reason to ask a specific question instead of silently inventing policy. Once a decision changes, update both the document and its behavior tests. Otherwise, documentation becomes another competing source of truth. 8. Give each task a path through the structure With the boundaries defined, a task can be precise without prescribing every implementation detail: Add an outstanding-balance display to the ticket card. Read the repository instructions and inspect the existing ticket flow. Expected behavior: - Show "Calculating" when outstandingMinor is null. - Show "Paid" when outstandingMinor is zero. - Otherwise format outstandingMinor using the ticket currency. Ownership: - The backend provides the authoritative balance. - The frontend formats and displays it. Scope: - Follow the existing API client and query conventions. - Do not change payment collection or billing finalization rules. - Identify missing contract information before implementing. Verification: - Cover null, zero, and positive outstanding balances. - Run the relevant application checks. - Summarize changed files, behavior, and remaining limitations. This gives the agent a destination, boundaries, and acceptance criteria. It still leaves room to inspect the code and choose the smallest appropriate implementation. 9. Enforce the rules that matter Instructions help an agent choose. Automated checks tell us when the result violates a rule. Rule Useful enforcement Cross-feature imports use public entry points ESLint restrictions or dependency-boundary tooling Client code must not import server-only implementation Server-only markers and framework build checks Frontend matches the API schema Type generation, type checking, and drift detection A user cannot access another tenant's ticket Integration or end-to-end authorization tests Payments remain correct under retries Idempotency and concurrency tests against the database The exact lint configuration depends on path aliases and repository layout. I would check both aliased and relative imports; blocking one spelling of a forbidden dependency is not enough. For payment work, a happy-path test is also insufficient. Two simultaneous requests can both pass a naive “remaining balance” check before either writes. That needs a deliberate database strategy and a test that exercises the race. Passing TypeScript proves something valuable about types. It does not prove authorization, accounting correctness, or concurrency safety. 10. Adopt this one feature at a time I would not stop delivery to reorganize the entire codebase. Start with a feature you already need to change: Identify its owner and existing conventions. Keep its implementation together. Define the entry points other features may use. Clarify the API fields that are easy to misinterpret. Add concise instructions and enforce the highest-value boundary. Then review an actual task. Did the agent find the existing API client? Did it preserve the business rule? Did the diff stay focused? Did the checks catch a meaningful failure? Those observations are more useful than assuming the new layout improved productivity. The structure is doing its job when a developer can open a feature, understand what it owns, and make a change without rediscovering the architecture. An AI coding agent benefits from the same clarity. Which boundary does your coding agent cross most often: feature imports, frontend/backend responsibilities, or business rules? References Next.js: Project structure and organization Next.js: Server and Client Components NestJS: Modules NestJS: OpenAPI introduction AGENTS.md Claude Code: Project memory and CLAUDE.md

title: Utiliser Claude Code avec Ollama sur Windows
author: CHAYMAE HANIDA
summary: Introduction Claude Code est un agent de programmation qui s'utilise dans le terminal. Ollama permet de lui fournir un modèle open source, y compris des modèles cloud gratuits. Dans cet article, je décris comment j'ai configuré les deux sur Windows et les problèmes rencontrés. Prérequis Windows 10 ou 11 PowerShell Un compte Ollama (gratuit) Une connexion internet Étape 1 : installer Claude Code Dans PowerShell : irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex Étape 2 : corriger le PATH Après l'installation, la commande claude n'était pas reconnue. Il faut ajouter le dossier d'installation au PATH : [ Environment ]:: SetEnvironmentVariable ( "Path" , [ Environment ]:: GetEnvironmentVariable ( "Path" , "User" ) + "; $ env : USERPROFILE \.local\bin" , "User" ) Fermer PowerShell, le rouvrir, puis vérifier : claude --version Étape 3 : installer Ollama Télécharger l'installateur sur ollama.com. Pour l'installer sur un autre disque : . \OllamaSetup.exe /DIR = "D:\Ollama" Pour stocker les modèles sur ce disque : [ Environment ]:: SetEnvironmentVariable ( "OLLAMA_MODELS" , "D:\OllamaModels" , "User" ) Se connecter ensuite à son compte Ollama depuis l'application. Étape 4 : lancer Claude Code avec Ollama mkdir D:\test-claude cd D:\test-claude ollama launch claude --model gemma4:31b-cloud Au premier lancement, Claude Code demande si on fait confiance au dossier. Il faut choisir Yes, I trust this folder (le choix par défaut est « No, exit »). Test J'ai demandé à Claude Code de créer un fichier : crée un fichier hello.py qui affiche Bonjour Résultat : le fichier hello.py a été créé avec le contenu suivant : print ( " Bonjour " ) Problème rencontré : modèle retiré Avec glm-5:cloud , j'ai obtenu l'erreur suivante : API Error: 410 glm-5 was retired on July 15, 2026 Les modèles cloud changent souvent. Pour voir la liste actuelle : ollama launch claude Utilisation dans VS Code En ouvrant le dossier du projet dans VS Code puis en lançant la commande depuis le terminal intégré, l'extension Claude Code pour VS Code s'installe automatiquement. Précautions Ne lancez pas Claude Code depuis C:\Users\<nom> : il aurait accès à tout votre dossier utilisateur. Utilisez toujours le dossier du projet. Le mode « auto » exécute des actions sans demander. Avec Shift + Tab , on peut choisir un mode qui demande une confirmation. Le modèle utilisé (ici Gemma 4) n'est pas Claude : la qualité des réponses diffère. Conclusion La configuration est rapide avec ollama launch claude . Les principales difficultés sont le PATH sous Windows et le choix d'un modèle cloud encore disponible.

title: From a Random Wheel to Reaction Time Tests: How I Ended Up Building Two Small Websites
author: Funny
summary: I spent quite a while trying to fix a twelve-sided die. The other dice worked fine. They rolled, bounced around, and eventually settled. But the D12 had a strange habit of stopping at an awkward angle, almost as if it couldn't stand up straight. Nothing was crashing. The result was correct. It just looked wrong. I probably could have left it alone, but once I'd noticed it, I couldn't really ignore it. So I went back to the code and kept adjusting things until the die finally behaved. That little problem came from a website I've been working on called WheelPage. I've also been building another site, PickTests, with small games that challenge your reaction time, memory, and attention. Both started as pretty simple ideas. I didn't really plan to build two websites with so many different things on them. It just happened one feature at a time. It started with a random wheel WheelPage began with a random wheel. You know those small decisions that aren't important enough to spend much time on, but somehow still take forever? What to eat for lunch, where to go with friends, or which name to pick from a list. I thought it would be fun to make a wheel that could handle those decisions. The first version of Spin the Wheel was straightforward. Type in a few options, click a button, watch the wheel spin, and get a result. It worked, which was enough to make me happy at first. But after using it a few times, I started noticing little things that were missing. If I entered a long list of names, I didn't want to type them all again the next day. And if I spun the wheel several times, it would be nice to look back at the previous results. So I added history, import and export options, sounds, animations, and a few ready-made lists. Then there was the mobile layout. Something that looked perfectly fine on my computer could feel cramped on a phone. The wheel needed enough space, but so did the buttons and the list of options. I'd adjust one part, check it on my phone, and end up changing something else. Eventually, I started thinking about other small random tools. Flip a Coin was an obvious one. When there are only two choices, a coin toss is simpler than setting up a wheel. I also made Rock Paper Scissors , where you can play a few rounds against the computer and keep track of your wins and losses. Then came the 3D Dice Roller . I didn't want it to be just a button that produced a random number. I wanted to see the dice actually roll. I used Three.js and Cannon-ES to handle the 3D graphics and physics. The tool now supports six types of dice, from D4 to D20, and lets you roll up to three at once. That's where the stubborn twelve-sided die from the beginning of this story came in. Getting the dice moving was one thing. Making sure they settled naturally was another. The code could run without errors and still produce something that looked a little strange. I use AI quite a bit while building these tools, and it helps me get things working faster. But I still have to open the page, try things out, and decide whether the result actually feels right. Later, I added a Random Number Generator and a Counter . They're more practical than the little games, but I liked having them in the same place. By then, WheelPage had grown from one wheel into six tools. I also made English, Chinese, Spanish, and Russian versions. I initially thought that would mostly involve translating the text. Turns out, a button that fits perfectly in one language can suddenly become too narrow in another. There are always little things like that. Then I made a reaction time test At some point, I wanted to try building something different. I've always liked those tiny browser games that take almost no time to understand but make you want to try again. A Reaction Time Test seemed like a good place to start. The idea is simple: wait for the screen to turn green, click as quickly as possible, and see how many milliseconds it took you to react. Maybe you get 280 ms on your first try and 250 ms on the next. Suddenly, you want to see if you can do better. I thought it would be an easy feature to build. Show a green screen, measure the time until the user clicks, and display the result. Of course, people don't always click exactly when they're supposed to. Someone might click before the screen turns green. Someone else might click several times in a row. And the whole thing needs to work with a mouse, keyboard, or touchscreen. None of these are huge problems on their own, but they still need to be handled. Once I had the basic test working, I noticed something else. Every time I took the test, I could only see my latest score. I couldn't easily remember what I'd scored earlier, let alone compare it with a previous session. So I added a five-round mode, along with average and best results. The site also keeps the most recent 20 completed tests in the browser. I decided not to add user accounts just for that. There is a downside, of course. If you clear your browser data or switch devices, your saved scores won't follow you. But for something you might play for a minute or two, I prefer letting people get straight into it without signing up. That reaction time test eventually became the starting point for my second website, PickTests. One small test turned into ten After finishing the reaction time test, I started experimenting with other ideas. First came Aim Trainer , where you try to hit targets as quickly and accurately as possible. Then I worked on a couple of memory games. In Sequence Memory , squares light up in a particular order, and you have to repeat the pattern. Number Memory asks you to remember a number and type it back after it disappears. They both involve memory, but they feel quite different to play. I also made Multiple Object Tracking . A few objects are marked, everything starts moving, and you have to keep track of the right ones. It's surprisingly easy to lose track when several objects cross paths. There are a few others too. The Stroop Test plays with the conflict between a word and the color it's displayed in. Time Perception lets you see how well you can judge time without watching a clock, while Mental Rotation is about recognizing shapes from different angles. I also added a Color Blind Test for a basic color-vision check. It's only an online screening activity, not a substitute for a professional eye examination. I built these pages using plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. I like keeping things fairly simple, although having more tests also means more things to look after. Each game has its own rules. Some measure time, some measure accuracy, and others track how far you manage to get. Even when two tests look similar, I can't always reuse the same approach. Still, it's been fun watching the collection grow. The tenth test was another small headache The latest addition is Schulte Table . If you haven't heard of it, the idea is pretty simple. You're given a grid of randomly arranged numbers, and you have to find them in order as quickly as you can. The usual version is a 5×5 grid with 25 numbers. I added different sizes, from 4×4 all the way to 9×9, along with a few different layouts. At first, I thought this one would be especially straightforward. Generate some numbers, shuffle them, let the user click in order, and measure the time. Then I got stuck on a small decision: what should happen if someone taps the wrong number? I could end the round immediately. That would be easy to understand, but it felt a bit harsh, especially on a phone where your finger might land on the wrong square. Ignoring mistakes entirely didn't seem quite right either. In the end, I decided to let the player continue while keeping a separate count of mistakes. The timer keeps running, and the final result shows both the completion time and the number of incorrect taps. I also had to keep records for different settings separate. Finding 16 numbers on a 4×4 grid isn't really comparable to finding 81 numbers on a 9×9 grid. And 81 numbers on a phone screen? That's another thing I still want to spend more time testing. The game is now live, and PickTests has reached ten tests. I'm still figuring out what to work on next Both websites are still small personal projects, and I'm still making changes. AI has definitely made it easier for me to try new ideas. If there's something I haven't built before, I can get a working version together much faster than I used to. But I also keep finding things I want to go back and improve. The D12 dice issue is fixed now. The reaction time test has better score history. Schulte Table is up and running, though I still want to spend more time checking how it feels on different devices. Sometimes I get an idea for another game and want to start building it right away. Then I open one of the existing pages and notice something I could make a little better. It's hard to choose between the two. For now, I haven't decided what the next test will be. I might just go back and work on the ones I've already made.

title: You can answer Claude Code's AskUserQuestion from a hook (and from your phone)
author: Dawon Lee
summary: Claude Code sometimes stops and asks you a multiple-choice question with the AskUserQuestion tool ("Which framework?", "Keep the old API or replace it?"). If you're away from the terminal, the run just sits there. The hooks docs describe answering it in -p mode: a PreToolUse hook returns allow plus an updatedInput that carries the answers. I wanted to know if the same works in a normal interactive session through a PermissionRequest hook, so I tested it on Claude Code 2.1.283. It does. What the hook receives When Claude calls AskUserQuestion in an interactive session, a PermissionRequest hook gets this on stdin (trimmed): { "hook_event_name" : "PermissionRequest" , "tool_name" : "AskUserQuestion" , "tool_input" : { "questions" : [ { "question" : "Which color do you want?" , "header" : "Color" , "options" : [ { "label" : "Red" , "description" : "red" }, { "label" : "Blue" , "description" : "blue" } ], "multiSelect" : false } ] } } What the hook returns Copy tool_input , add an answers object that maps each question's text to the chosen label (comma-separated for multi-select), and return it as updatedInput with behavior: "allow" : { "hookSpecificOutput" : { "hookEventName" : "PermissionRequest" , "decision" : { "behavior" : "allow" , "updatedInput" : { "questions" : [ ...same as input... ], "answers" : { "Which color do you want?" : "Blue" } } } } } Claude Code then shows: ⏺ User answered Claude's questions: ⎿ · Which color do you want? → Blue ⎿ Allowed by PermissionRequest hook and Claude continues with "Blue". No terminal prompt appears. A minimal test hook #!/bin/sh # Answers every AskUserQuestion with the last option. For testing only. python3 -c ' import json, sys d = json.load(sys.stdin) if d.get("tool_name") != "AskUserQuestion": sys.exit(0) # no decision: the normal permission prompt shows ti = d["tool_input"] ti["answers"] = {q["question"]: q["options"][-1]["label"] for q in ti.get("questions", [])} print(json.dumps({"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "PermissionRequest", "decision": {"behavior": "allow", "updatedInput": ti}}})) ' Register it under hooks.PermissionRequest in a settings file and try claude --settings test-settings.json . Two things to watch allow alone doesn't answer the question. If your approval hook (or an approval app) just returns allow for AskUserQuestion , the question stays open and the session still waits. I hit exactly this: my phone approval said "allowed", but Claude was still waiting. The hook blocks until it returns. To answer from somewhere else, the hook has to wait for that answer (and give up before the hook timeout so the terminal prompt still works). Using it from a phone I build Lidnight , a menu bar app that keeps a Mac awake while Claude Code and Codex work. Version 1.7.79 uses this: when Claude asks a question, the options show up on the phone status page (end-to-end encrypted) and in the Mac menu bar, and the one you tap goes back to Claude through the hook. You can still answer in the terminal; whichever comes first wins.
